metadata.root: Optional. Shared id linking entries descended from one root (e.g. 'dragan'); siblings wake together.

candidates.note: 'a leaf, a thin plate', from petalos 'outspread, broad, flat'.
candidates.editorial_notes: Checked 2026-10-02 (etymonline, Wiktionary). Verdict (2026-10-02): KIN ONLY, not to be promoted on its own. Claims all confirmed, but the image is thin; better as kin under fathom than as its own entry. English petala 1704, petal 1726, from Modern Latin petalum. Root *peth2- (PIE), with fathom and patent. Revisit if the interface shows root families.

candidates.note: en- 'put in' + trance, from Old French transe 'passage from life to death; swoon', from transir 'to pass on, die', from Latin transire 'to go across'. To be entranced (1590s) was to be thrown into a passing-away, a swoon like a little death.
candidates.editorial_notes: Checked 2026-10-02 (etymonline entrance, trance; Wiktionary). Verdict: sound, but HOLD: the engine matches spelling, so the common noun 'the entrance' (a different word, from French entrer, 1520s) would take this gloss. Needs sense by part of speech. Usually seen as 'entranced'. Wiktionary labels transe Anglo-Norman. Missing from both homonym lists; reason unchecked.

candidates.note: 'a hole in the ice' (Old Norse vǫk), probably via Middle Low German or Middle Dutch wake; the sense perhaps came via the track a vessel cuts through ice.
candidates.editorial_notes: Checked 2026-10-02 (etymonline, Wiktionary Etymology 3). Verdict: sound with its hedges, but HOLD: the engine would gloss the verb 'wake' and 'wake up' as 'open channel'. Shortlist row 99, unmarked on the review page. Correction: the ship's wake is NOT kin to wake (rouse) and wake (the vigil, Old English -wacu 'a watching'), which share PIE *weg- 'lively'. Wiktionary traces the ship's wake to Proto-Germanic *wakwō 'wetness', PIE *wegʷ- 'wet'. Never imply kinship with waking. Figurative 'in the wake of' 1806-1822, 'following close behind'.

candidates.note: vet, short for veterinarian (Latin veterinarius 'of beasts of burden'); the verb (1891) was first stock-trading and racing slang for putting an animal under a vet's care; by 1901 any careful examination.
candidates.editorial_notes: Checked 2026-10-02 (etymonline vet, veterinarian; Wiktionary veterinus; Lewis & Short). Verdict: HOLD, leaning reject. The image is weak (vet = animal doctor is not hidden), Wiktionary hedges the verb's derivation ('possibly by analogy'), and 'the vet' (veteran, 1848) would misfire. Veterinarius 'of beasts of burden' is confirmed; 'horse' narrows it (De Vaan: veterinus usually of equines). The interesting image belongs to veterinarian, contested: veterinae perhaps from vetus 'old' (experienced, or a yearling, strong enough to draw loads; De Vaan EDL p. 673: 'the old stock'), or from vehō 'to carry' (Lewis & Short; Wiktionary 'semantically better'). Any such entry needs both theories, each marked 'perhaps'.
